fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. King Agrippa and Bernice, who comes with him, came down to Caesarea "…to pay their respects to Festus," the Roman governor there. It was a courtesy call. Even kings drop by to say hello.

No feast is mentioned here, friend. The text says King Agrippa and Bernice, who comes with him, came down to pay their respects to Festus, the Roman governor of Caesarea. No party, no cookie table, just a visit to a person.

Right, friend. Festus says it's not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has had an opportunity to face his accusers. He told this to the chief priests and elders of the Jews, who had asked for a judgment against Paul. In Festus's words, the man gets the chance to face the people pointing the finger.

Family isn't in the verse, friend. Festus says a man must have an opportunity to face his accusers, the people bringing the charges against him. That's who the custom is about. The word family never shows up, so that seat stays empty.
Jailers aren't in the verse. Festus says the man has an opportunity to face his accusers, the ones bringing the charges against him. He said this to the chief priests and elders of the Jews.

Hide isn't the word here. Festus says the man has an opportunity to defend himself against the charges. He told this to the chief priests and elders of the Jews. That's the custom as Festus describes it.

That's it, baker. Festus says the contentions were about "…a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Paul, the apostle, is the one affirming it. I think that's a bold thing to say.
Not this one. Festus says the contentions were about a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul "…affirmed to be alive." The word is alive, not innocent. That's what Paul, the apostle, affirmed.

Not what the verse says. Festus says the contentions were regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Nothing there says Jesus was forgotten. The word is alive.

You got it, baker. Festus, the Roman governor, tells King Agrippa, "Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters…" he asked Paul about going to Jerusalem to be tried there. Honestly, I respect a man who admits he's lost. I once spent a whole morning hunting for my own apron while I was wearing it.

Festus doesn't say that. He says he was "…at a loss as to how to investigate these matters" so he asked Paul whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there. The reason he gives is being at a loss. A report to Jerusalem isn't mentioned.
Yes, friend. Paul appealed to the Emperor, and Festus says he ordered Paul held "…until I could send him to Caesar." Caesar is the title for the Emperor. Festus is telling this part to King Agrippa.

Ooh, Felix, I see you looking at that name, friend. Festus says in verse 14 that Felix is the man who left Paul in prison. He came before Festus (Acts 24:27). The one Paul is being sent to is Caesar, and verse 21 says so.

King Agrippa is the one Festus is talking to, but he isn't who Paul is being sent to. Festus says he'd hold Paul "…until I could send him to Caesar." Agrippa is who Festus tells the story to. Paul's appeal was to the Emperor.

I see why you'd flip it, friend, but the text says otherwise. After hearing Festus, King Agrippa says, "I would like to hear this man myself." Festus answers, "Tomorrow you will hear him…" Agrippa is the one who asked, and Festus says yes.

Not here, baker. The text says Agrippa and Bernice came "…with great pomp…" and entered the auditorium along with the commanders and leading men of the city. Quiet isn't the word the text gives. Pomp is.

The text doesn't tell us what Agrippa and Bernice wore. It says they came "…with great pomp…" and entered along with the commanders and leading men of the city. Plain clothes isn't in the verse. Pomp is the word we get.

Yes. Festus says the whole Jewish community petitioned him, "…crying out that he ought not to live any longer." This is a heavy one. Keep your eye on what Festus says next about Paul, because it matters.
That's not in the text. Festus says they were "…crying out that he ought not to live any longer." Whipping and release isn't what he reports. It's a heavy line, and I'll leave it as the text has it.
